articles.title: More young hikers lost using Google Maps on Lake District fells, say rescuers
articles.summary: Lake District mountaineering instructors say more education on navigation will help on the fells.
articles.body:
More young people are getting caught out on the fells due to relying on Google Maps for navigation, rescuers have said.

After a full-team rescue on Sunday, Wasdale Mountain Rescue Team (WMRT) said an increasing amount of young people, mostly aged 18 to 24, were getting lost or into trouble after using Google Maps on their phones.

WMRT said Google Maps was "not made for the mountains", because unlike a paper map, the app does not display steep rocky outcrops, fell paths and contours, which show three-dimensional shape of the land.

The advice to use a paper map - which is echoed by Google - has been repeated by rescue teams for years, so how can navigation be made more available to young people?

"It's a tricky one," mountaineering and climbing instructor (MCI) Pippa Archer, who lives in Kendal, said.

"I can see the appeal of using something that is free and readily available on your phone, however, a map and compass won't set you back too much," she said.

Archer, who guides and helps people develop their skills in the mountains, said the detail on a paper map was "crucial for staying safe" and "gives a picture of what to expect on your walk, and this is the key to not getting lost".

"A walking map will show you where the ground gets really steep, where there are cliffs to avoid, or streams that need to be crossed," she said.

"The apparent increase in Google Maps use in mountain environments may reflect changing navigation habits rather than simply poor preparation or judgement," winter mountain leader and MCI James Anstee said.

Anstee, who lives in Windermere, said the app's "familiarity and reliability in everyday settings may create an assumption that it is equally suitable for the mountains", without full appreciation of what the terrain demands.

"The challenge is therefore as much about awareness and education as it is about technology," he said.

He said encouraging people to understand limitations of navigation applications, learning about terrain and appropriate navigational competence was "likely to be more beneficial than simply discouraging the use of a particular app".

As a secondary choice for navigation on the phone, WMRT recommended OS Maps, Hiiker or Outdooractive apps which were made for walkers.

Even with the rise of digital devices in recent years, Archer said a compass and a map were still the safest tools, as apps can freeze without signal or could need an update while up on the fell with no phone signal.

It comes as three men needed help on Sunday after they got lost walking from Scafell Pike using Google Maps, which had not updated, rescuers said.

Archer said: "If I used my phone for all my navigation it would quickly run the battery down, compromising my safety if I did need to call for rescue.

"I only use a navigation app for two purposes: to quickly pinpoint my position, or to zoom in to see the map better," she said, and advised people to take screen shots of a map as a back up.

Archer said: "I know some people worry they don't know how to use a compass, but the main thing to remember is that the red end of the needle always points north.

"Knowing this then allows you to work out which way is east, south, west or north, and combining this knowledge with the map allows you to select the right path down from the summit."

Archer advised those getting to grips with navigation to "head out on a route that you know, but take a walking map with you, and see if you can piece together how the land around you is represented on the map".

"You'll probably need a few pointers as you bring in the compass, so head out with a more experienced friend or sign up for a one-day navigation course," she said.

A Google spokesperson said the company's map app was designed for streets and that it "calculated estimated time of arrivals based on standard walking speeds and showed clear warnings that conditions may vary".

"We encourage hikers to use trail maps and apps designed specifically for hiking," they said.

articles.summary: An at-home DNA test gifted for a birthday has reunited two long-lost brothers after nearly 80 years, revealing a family connection between Canada and the
articles.body: An at-home DNA test gifted for a birthday has reunited two long-lost brothers after nearly 80 years, revealing a family connection between Canada and the Netherlands. Frank McGrath, 78, from Quebec, discovered that Frans Bannink, 80, living in the Dutch city of Almelo, was his older half-brother after Bannink’s granddaughter uncovered a Canadian family link through a MyHeritage DNA test. The discovery led to their first meeting in Amsterdam in April 2025, where the brothers found striking physical similarities and an immediate connection. Their shared father was a Canadian soldier stationed in the Netherlands after the Second World War.How did an at-home DNA test reunite two brothers after 80 yearsAccording to Global News, Hogervorst explained that her grandfather had initially been reluctant to discover the identity of his biological father. However, after spotting the Canadian connection in the DNA results, she decided to reach out to McGrath. She said: “When I saw the connection on the website, I immediately sent Frank a message and he responded some weeks later.”The message eventually led to contact between the two families and arrangements for a meeting. McGrath, who had grown up believing he was an only child, said the discovery was particularly emotional. Speaking to Global News, he recalled: “It was very emotional for me. I was very happy.” He added: “Having been brought up an only child, to find out I had an older brother … and a brother who looks like our father.”What did the DNA test reveal about the brothers’ Canadian fatherThe DNA discovery revealed that both men had the same father, Staff Sgt. Dermot McGrath, a Canadian soldier who had been stationed in the Netherlands after the country's liberation during the Second World War. Dermot McGrath met Frank's mother several years after Frans Bannink was born, although the circumstances surrounding the two relationships had remained unknown to Frank.McGrath told Global News that his father had never spoken about Bannink. He said: “He didn’t know. He never talked about it.” He also explained that his father had been married to his mother for 60 years before she died, adding: “That was his loyalty. If he had known … we all would have known.” The discovery therefore brought to light a family connection that had remained undiscovered for decades.What happened when the brothers finally met in AmsterdamThe brothers arranged their first face-to-face meeting in Amsterdam in April 2025. McGrath travelled to the Netherlands, where he and his newly discovered brother spent four days together. Recalling their first encounter, McGrath told Global News: “We landed in Amsterdam and rented a hotel near Frans’ home. We met every day for four days. We had some really good times.”Bannink also recalled the moment he first saw McGrath at the hotel. He said: “He came downstairs at the hotel and I said, ‘There’s the guy.’ It was instant.” Their families also noticed physical similarities and shared mannerisms between the brothers. The two men even had strikingly similar names: Frans and Francis, although McGrath is commonly known as Frank.What happened after the brothers reunited following 80 yearsThe reunion also brought together relatives who had previously been unaware of one another. McGrath's wife, Johanne Tremblay McGrath, described the immediate connection between the families, saying: “It was an instant connection between the two of them, and also us.” She also spoke about meeting her new sister-in-law, adding: “Same values, we are both huggers, and both criers.”The discovery has since established a relationship between the two families, who are now looking forward to spending time together. The families were separated by thousands of kilometres before the DNA discovery brought them into contact. What began with a birthday gift and a DNA test ultimately revealed the brothers' shared family history and allowed them to meet after nearly 80 years without knowing each other existed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Romney Marsh Community hub to close citing financial challenges
articles.summary: Lisa Green, who works in the cafe, says the team is like a "family" and people rely on the hub.
articles.body:
A cook at a community hub cafe has said she feels "punched in the stomach" after learning services will close following a decision to place the organisation into administration.

The trustees of Romney Marsh Community Hub, which supports the over 50s, said significant financial challenges meant services were being brought to an end, with administrators to be appointed within days .

Lisa Green, a cook at the charity's Hub on the Beach cafe, said the hub helped people dealing with bereavement, arthritis, cancer and other needs.

Kent County Council (KCC) said decisions were a matter for the charity's trustees, but it was in contact to understand the impact and help people access support.

Lisa said one customer brought her mother, who has dementia, to the cafe every Saturday and saw it as a "lifeline", but she'd had to explain to her parent, who was now "really quite confused", that it was closing.

"There are so many people that rely on us," she said. "Some people haven't got anyone."

Lisa baked for the cafe, making old-fashioned puddings and cakes such as Victoria sponges that she said appealed to older customers.

She said staff, who had rent and mortgages to pay, had been told they were not going to get paid, but added: "It's more than that… We're like a big family down there."

On Facebook, the cafe said it could not open from Friday without " a miracle "

Rye's Sunflower Charity Shop, which supported the hub, also said: " Our beloved shop will be closing with immediate effect ."

Kent councillor David Wimble has said work is ongoing to explore whether a rescue proposal can be developed.

Businesses in Romney Marsh High Street are collecting signatures for a petition.

Tony Vaughan, Folkestone and Hythe MP, said he was " deeply saddened " by the closure and claimed council cuts to a wellbeing contract had contributed to the charity's difficulties.

He said that some services had already found new homes .

A KCC spokeswoman said the authority recognised the important role the hub played in supporting older and vulnerable residents, through community, wellbeing and transport services.

She said changes to community wellbeing services in April led to reduced spending and a lower-value contract for Social Enterprise Kent, which delivers wellbeing services on behalf of KCC.

"We recognise the particular challenges faced by rural communities such as Romney Marsh, including transport barriers and access to local services," she said.

"We will continue to work with Romney Marsh Community Hub and partners to assess the impact of these developments and help residents to alternative sources of support where possible."

articles.title: Breast Friends Solihull honoured with King's award for volunteers
articles.summary: The King's Award for Voluntary Service is the highest award given to voluntary groups in the UK.
articles.body:
Annette Farrington-Moore says a charity became a lifeline after her breast cancer diagnosis, and now the group that helped her is celebrating a major milestone with a royal seal of approval.

Run by volunteers with lived experience of the disease, Breast Friends Solihull provides emotional and practical support with many involved forging lifelong friendships.

"You don't want to trouble family and they don't really understand what you're going through emotionally," she said.

"The kids were there for me but when I found out about Breast Friends it was like the best thing ever."

Those who run the group firmly believe that no-one should go through breast cancer alone.

The organisation has supported thousands of people affected by breast cancer over the last 25 years, and has juar been awarded the King's Award for Voluntary Service.

Annette, 64, was diagnosed with breast cancer last year. Widowed and feeling low, she found solace in attending meetings and events put on by the group.

"Whenever you're ill and you haven't got your husband, there's no one there to look after you like they would," she said.

"So having Breast Friends, you know there's somebody on the end of the phone who can be there for you."

The charity provides services such as gardening and cleaning to allow people to rest during treatment, as well as support with bras, wigs and hospital visits.

It has also raised money to fund hospital equipment.

Chris Pile was diagnosed with breast cancer 20 years ago, when she was a nurse and mother of two young children.

She is now vice-chair of the group and helps lift others when they're down.

"I joined Breast Friends when I finished my chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and I found it really uplifting," she explained.

Everybody was so positive and friendly, and I got involved straight away because that's the kind of person I am.

"I've organised days and nights out, summer suppers and the Christmas dos."

Chair Deborah Douglas has had breast cancer twice, first in 2003 and again earlier this year.

She said she has now been given "the all clear" following treatment.

Her experiences mean she knows first-hand what support to offer, explaining that a diagnosis can be "scary and frightening".

Her first diagnosis led her to seek help from Breast Friends.

"I walked in and I saw women who weren't sad. They were all happy and so uplifting, and they basically supported me from the moment I walked in.

"It was such an uplifting experience, and I always leave Breast Friends smiling," she added.

"We laugh, but we also talk about our issues and how we're feeling.

"That emotional support is so important because the people around you know exactly what you're going through. People don't always want to share those things with their family."

More than 20 years on, she is still involved as the group's chair.

articles.title: Could lack of a tourist tax benefit Gloucestershire?
articles.summary: Businesses in the county say they oppose introducing the levy as hospitality is already struggling.
articles.body:
Hospitality businesses in Gloucestershire say the lack of a tourism tax in the county could give it a competitive edge when it comes to attracting visitors.

The government's proposed overnight visitor lev y would allow councils and regional authorities to charge holidaymakers an additional fee for their accommodation, raising money to be spent on local services.

But Gloucestershire is not currently eligible to introduce the charge due to the set-up of local government there.

Naomi Hands, director of the Speech House Hotel in the Forest of Dean, said introducing the tourist tax would add more pressure onto an already struggling industry.

Campaigning mum awarded honorary doctorate

Major tourist cities such as Paris, Rome and Brussels already have their own version of a tourist tax, as does Edinburgh in Scotland.

The levy would allow councils to use the money raised to invest in local facilities such as parks, high streets and public toilets.

The plans have attracted criticism from those working in hospitality, who argue visitors are already facing rising costs and that another charge could make domestic holidays less affordable.

Hands said: "You can only charge what people are reasonably prepared to spend."

She argued the absence of a levy in Gloucestershire could potentially work in the county's favour, particularly as holidaymakers look for more affordable UK destinations.

Phil Kiernan, who runs the Farmers Boy Inn on the edge of the Forest of Dean, also says introducing that a tourism tax would place further pressure on already struggling rural businesses.

"I've been here for 27 years and it's never been harder than it is now," he said.

He added: "We're already dealing with rising business rates, rising minimum wages, increased employers costs, energy bills and VAT. And now we're being told there might be another tax we would have to impose on our guests," he said.

"I'm completely, 150% opposed to introducing any tourism tax, particularly in rural areas."

David Weston, chair of the UK Bed and Breakfast Association, has also questioned the proposal, arguing that taxing people for taking holidays in the UK does not make sense when the hospitality sector is already under pressure.

But local leaders argue that visitors should contribute towards the cost of maintaining the places they come to enjoy.

Cllr Julie Jones-Evans, chair of the Local Government Authority's Culture, Tourism and Sport Committee, said: "When designed locally, a visitor levy can directly support tourism businesses and strengthen the visitor economy in our communities."

Neighbouring local authorities who are eligible to implement the tax include the West of England Combined Authority (Weca).

It appears likely the tax will be introduced in cities such as Bristol and Bath.

West of England mayor Helen Godwin said: "Now is the time to look at making sure we can invest more in what matters through a small charge on overnight stays here."

The debate over tourism funding comes as popular destinations face growing concerns about the impact of visitor numbers on local communities.

The proposed tourism levy would also allow non-mayoral Foundation Strategic Authorities to introduce a levy, meaning an elected mayor would not be required.

Six of Gloucestershire's seven councils have previously expressed an ambition to establish a strategic authority for the county by May 2027.

However, Gloucestershire has not yet secured a devolution deal, and its future arrangements remain subject to government decisions.

The government has previously said it would protect budget holidays by "ensuring low-cost accommodation pays the lowest levy."

The proposals are intended to give mayors greater control over funding for local improvements, with the Government previously suggesting the tourism levy could be introduced by March of 2028.

articles.summary: The DOJ said the alleged ring targeted "high-value" trains traveling through Southern California that carried shoes, tools, and other products.
articles.body:
Federal prosecutors announced charges against 14 people on Nov. 19 in connection with an alleged cargo theft ring accused of targeting at least three dozen trains in Southern California and stealing more than $22 million in merchandise, including Nike sneakers and Milwaukee tools.

The Justice Department said the alleged ring targeted "high-value" trains traveling through Southern California that carried shoes, tools, and other products. The group allegedly coordinated the thefts via Instagram and sold the stolen goods on the black market.

"The scale of the theft is staggering. We have charged a crew of 14 in a scheme to steal more than $22.5 million in cargo from at least three dozen freight trains in Southern California," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli in a released statement. "We will prosecute the people who raid these trains and those who knowingly turn stolen cargo into cash."

According to the Justice Department, the ring operated from February 2024 to August 2026 and organized its thefts through Instagram messages. Prosecutors said Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles, led the ring.

At least 36 trains were burglarized during the operation, the Justice Department said, with the group targeting trains carrying valuable merchandise that routinely arrives through the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, California. The burglaries occurred in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, and other locations in Southern California.

Members of the alleged ring cut air hoses on the trains they targeted, forcing them to come to an emergency stop, prosecutors said. The stolen train cargo was later loaded into trucks and vans and transported to stash houses.

According to prosecutors, members of the ring allegedly sold more than $1 million in stolen Nike sneakers and other merchandise to an unnamed Los Angeles-based sneaker and streetwear resale company in 2025. Others advertised the stolen merchandise on social media.

Federal prosecutors on Nov. 14 identified the people who were charged in the case:

Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, of East Los Angeles

Daniel Angel, 38, aka "Rayo," of East Los Angeles (Nathan Angel's father)

Rodolfo Angel, 23, aka "Rudy" and "Flaco," of East Los Angeles (Nathan Angel's uncle)

Jose Luis Angel, 23, aka "Joe," of East Los Angeles

Donta Hedgeman, 27, aka "Dret," of East Los Angeles

Fernando Alexis Alvarado Villegas, 27, of Los Angeles

Carlos Robert Estrada, 28, aka "JD," of Whittier, California

Angel Sanchez, 24, aka "Fluffy," of Commerce, California

Ruben Mario Banuelos, 26, aka "Bubu," of East Los Angeles

Fredy Marquina, 25, of the Westlake neighborhood of Los Angeles

Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez, 23, of Los Angeles

Jorge Angel Aguilar Espinoza, 36, of East Los Angeles

All 14 were charged with one count of conspiracy. The indictment also includes 14 counts of theft of interstate railroad cargo and possession or receipt of stolen interstate railroad cargo, and two counts of violence against railroad carriers.

A lawyer for the defendants had not been listed in the court record as of Nov. 19. If convicted, they face a statutory maximum sentence of five years in federal prison for the conspiracy count, up to 10 years for each theft count, and a statutory maximum sentence of life in federal prison for each violence against railroad cars count.

"This historic indictment, following a 14-month investigation assisted by our Bureau of Investigation, demonstrates the importance of dismantling entire criminal enterprises," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman in a released statement. "We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market."

articles.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.summary: People stocking up on long-life food drove retail sales higher October, according to official data.
articles.body:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying .

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.

The latest official sales figures from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.

Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".

Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.

Sales of tinned food and bottled water jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch

Why should I stockpile and what will I need?

Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.

Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said.

Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.

Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.

These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.

Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

articles.title: Calls for consent law change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.summary: Joanne Young's daughter joins her mother in calling for a change to the law on consent.
articles.body:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change to the law on consent.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period , using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials of this nature.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone.

"We live in a world where someone's partner can consent for them, and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.

"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.

"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."

The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

"If someone is drugged asleep and unconscious they can't give consent," Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC.

"Someone can't give consent on your behalf.

"[Technology] is quickly evolving but we need to look at where improvements can be made in the legislation."

Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.

"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.

"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."

Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.

"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.

"So why are they still accessible?" she said.

Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.

"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.

"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."

Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.

"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.

"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help us others when this has happened to them."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line .

Horvath said more needed to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.

"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.

"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.

"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."

Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told LBC that she did not believe it would be the last unless changes were made.

"The ability of these men to find each other on websites that you and I could just log on to now just means that these cases are going to keep on coming," she said.

"The state needs to make sure that its online safety laws and regulations are strong enough to stop this from ever being able to happen," she said.

"I think that every single one of the websites listed in this case should be called on today to answer the questions, can you guarantee this isn't happening today?"

Phillips said there was "absolutely" a case for making it an offence to advertise another person for sex online and that exploitation of adults occurs "all across the internet" with "very little regulation on the safety or the certainty of consent".

The Domestic Abuse Commissioner, Dame Nicole Jacobs, has also called for the case to be a "turning point":

"Ultimately this case again highlights that we need to stop treating drug-facilitated sexual abuse as an isolated incident and recognise it for the form of horrific domestic abuse that it is," she said.

The men who committed crimes against Joanne Young are:

Philip Young pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife

Norman Macksoni, 48, from Bedfordshire, and Richard Wilkins, 62, from Swindon, were each found guilty of one count of rape. Wilkins was also found guilty of one count of assault by penetration

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, from Swindon, was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration

Mohammed Hassan, 38, from Swindon, was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February

articles.title: 'His name is Siraj': Congress MP Imran Masood on why pacer wasn't picked for India vs NZ Test; BJP hits back
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The selection of India's playing XI has triggered a face-off between the Congress and the BJP, with the opposition alleging discrimination
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The selection of India's playing XI has triggered a face-off between the Congress and the BJP, with the opposition alleging discrimination against pacer Mohammed Siraj and the ruling party accusing it of dragging communal politics into cricket.The exchange began after India’s team management opted for a four-pronged pace attack but left out Siraj against New Zealand, despite the Hyderabad pacer’s impressive record and reputation for delivering in challenging conditions.Congress MP Imran Masood questioned Siraj’s exclusion, suggesting that his religious identity could have played a role in the decision."His name is Siraj -- isn't that reason enough? If he is performing and still not getting selected, what else could be the reason behind it? This alone can be the reason; there can be no other reason besides this," Masood told news agency IANS.In another interaction, the Congress MP said it was being pointed out that Siraj had performed well but was still not included in the team. "If you are not selecting him despite his good performance, the discrimination is clear," he told news agency ANI.The BJP was quick to hit back, accusing the Congress of turning team selection into a communal issue and using cricket for vote-bank politics.BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said, "Shame on Congress! Congress now does vote bank politics even in Cricket team selection! Congress says - 'Siraj was left out because he was a Muslim'."Pointing out that all-rounder Ravindra Jadeja had also been left out, Bhandari said, "Every cricketer wears the jersey representing India! Stop dividing Indian cricket team for vote bank and communal politics!"Why Siraj's exclusion has raised eyebrowsSiraj's omission has also drawn attention because of the role he has played in India's pace attack over the past few years.Fifteen months ago, on a cloudy morning in London, Siraj stepped out of Jasprit Bumrah's shadow to produce one of the most memorable performances of his career. The pacer emptied the tank on the final day of a gruelling five-Test series to help India secure a 2-2 draw against England at The Oval.His performance appeared to signal the beginning of a new phase in his career, with Siraj emerging as a potential leader of India's pace attack as Bumrah entered an intensive workload management programme.However, the pacer was left out on Thursday despite conditions in Wellington appearing tailor-made for seam bowling. The team management instead went ahead with four other seamers.One possible reason for the decision could be Siraj's recent form. His underwhelming performance against Sri Lanka in the Colombo Test three months ago may have prompted the team management to reassess his place in the playing XI.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Queen Elizabeth II's former dressmaker once used a Cotswolds estate as his weekend retreat; its renovated 3,239-square-foot guest barn is now listed for £1.5 million, below its 2024 purchase price
articles.summary: A stone barn in the English countryside that once served as a weekend guest house for Queen Elizabeth II's dressmaker is now on the market for £1.5
articles.body: A stone barn in the English countryside that once served as a weekend guest house for Queen Elizabeth II's dressmaker is now on the market for £1.5 million. The four-bedroom property in Langford, in the Cotswolds, has recently been renovated and is being sold for £50,000 less than the price its current owners paid for it in October 2024.The property, known as Hardy's Barn, was once part of the country estate of Sir Hardy Amies, the fashion designer who worked for Queen Elizabeth II for decades. As reported by Mansion Global, the converted barn has 3,239 square feet of living space and stands on about 0.39 acres. According to the report, estate agent Butler Sherborn began marketing the property at the end of October. The sellers bought it for £1.55 million in October 2024 and have since carried out a major renovation. Their identities were not disclosed in the report.A country retreat for the Queen's dressmakerHardy Amies was one of Britain's best-known fashion designers and founded the Hardy Amies fashion house. He first worked with Queen Elizabeth II in 1950 and was appointed her official dressmaker and a holder of a Royal Warrant in 1955.Although his professional work was based in London, Amies spent most weekends in Langford, a small village in the Cotswolds. The barn formed part of his estate and was used as a guest house. According to property consultancy Butler Sherborn, the contrast between his London work and weekends in the countryside influenced his approach to design.Amies created several outfits for the Queen, including the well-known pink dress she wore during her Silver Jubilee celebrations in 1977. His work extended beyond royal clothing. He also designed the outfits for England's 1966 World Cup-winning football team, the 1972 British Olympic team and costumes for the film 2001: A Space Odyssey. The guest house is now named Hardy's Barn after the designer.What the renovated property looks likeAccording to the current listing, the 3,239-square-foot home combines original features with modern interiors. The entrance opens into a large open-plan area that brings together the kitchen, dining space and living room. Exposed wooden ceiling beams remain a prominent feature, alongside herringbone flooring and a wood-burning stove. The kitchen has sage-green cabinets.The living area opens into an orangery, which leads to a separate snug. There is also a boot room near the entrance and a study with a large skylight. The property has four bedrooms and two bathrooms. One bedroom is on the ground floor, while the other three are upstairs. The main bedroom has a dressing room and an attached bathroom with a separate shower and bathtub.Outside, the house sits on approximately 0.39 acres. Its grounds include a south-west-facing garden, mature trees and views across the surrounding countryside. The listing also mentions driveway parking.Listed below its previous purchase priceThe £1.5 million asking price is slightly lower than the £1.55 million paid by the current owners in October 2024. The reduction comes after the renovation, although the sellers' reasons for putting the property back on the market have not been disclosed.The property is listed as a freehold barn conversion in Langford, Oxfordshire. Its combination of historic features, updated interiors and connection to a well-known royal designer makes it different from an ordinary countryside home. For buyers interested in the Cotswolds, the property offers a renovated family house with a history linked to one of the designers who shaped Queen Elizabeth II's public wardrobe.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russia targets Kyiv crossings days after Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
articles.summary: Russia launched one of its biggest air attacks yet as it rejected the prospect of security guarantees for Ukraine.
articles.body:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.

Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.

Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".

The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.

At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.

Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".

Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.

The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.

The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.

Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.

He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.

The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit €70bn (£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.

The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.

On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country .

It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.

Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.

Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.

France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.

He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

articles.title: Cyprus opened MUSAN in 2021 with 93 sculptures to help rewild a resort seabed; early algae and fish appeared, but recent reports say colonisation remains limited
articles.summary: Explore the journey of MUSAN in Ayia Napa, Cyprus, where underwater sculptures aim to rewild the seabed and attract marine life, though growth has been slower than anticipated.
articles.body: Most statues are meant to stay the same. However, the ones off Ayia Napa in Cyprus were made to change over time. When the Museum of Underwater Sculpture Ayia Napa, or MUSAN, opened in 2021, its 93 sculptures were meant to help rewild a bare patch of seabed next to a busy resort. A few years later, the picture is a mixed bag. According to the Cyprus Mail, algae and some fish have moved in. Still, the museum's creator says life has arrived more slowly than he had hoped.Trees on the sand British sculptor Jason deCaires Taylor created MUSAN both as a piece of art and as a home for marine life. Many of his sculptures look like trees sprouting out of the seabed, and that was his intention. Branches provide shelter for the animals at various depths within an open, sandy environment. Sculptures were built from pH-neutral, environmentally friendly materials, so there won't be any harm to the sea. The museum itself is located within a protected zone where fishing is not allowed. The plan looked good on paper. Taylor said that watching the work change over time was central to its meaning. He wanted still, grey statues to transform into living structures.Signs of lifeSome of that change is now easy to see. The same report said Cyprus’s Department of Fisheries and Marine Research had found several kinds of algae on parts of the installation. A large number of oysters had settled, especially on top of some sculptures. Michalis Konias, who runs the visitor centre, told the paper that the growth had become very clear. He also noted that fish activity had increased in recent years, and Taylor added that the visibility there was among the clearest he had ever seen. Green and loggerhead turtles and Mediterranean monk seals have also been seen near the museum.Why the pace feels slow Despite the early growth of algae and oysters, fish colonisation lagged behind Taylor's expectations. He described the transformation at MUSAN as “notably subtle and slow,” adding that the relative absence of species, particularly fish, was sticking. He had expected to see more marine life, particularly around the tree structures. In the Atlantic, at a similar latitude, he said that a tree structure he installed attracted thousands of fish within two years. However, nothing like that had happened at MUSAN yet. He pointed to decades of overfishing in the Mediterranean. A 2022 Journal of Marine Science and Engineering paper by Rallis and colleagues surveyed concrete reefs off Crete three times over the five years after they were placed there in 2015. Over 80% of the surface was covered with algae each time. The authors mention that the area is low in nutrients, which makes it difficult for large, fast-growing organisms to develop. That study, however, was in Greece and looked at seabed plants and small animals, not fish. So it only gives a clue.What to watch next Taylor described the typical sequence for submerged structures. First, a slight colour change occurs as algae and calcareous organisms settle, then crustaceans in crevices and finally juvenile fish. Juvenile fish are usually the permanent residents who arrive in search of a refuge from predators. MUSAN is well past the early stages. The harder test is whether the fish are settling in numbers, especially around the tree forms. The same report's list of species seen near the site includes squid, common octopus and Pterois miles, the lionfish, a non-native predator. For Taylor, unpredictability is part of the point. Once a sculpture is underwater, he says, its future is no longer his to direct.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A father and his 11-year-old son set Guinness World Records for daring parking and drifting stunts; then dad donated his record-breaking Mini Cooper for public display
articles.summary: A British stunt driver and his 11-year-old son turned their shared passion for cars into a family achievement by setting three Guinness World Records
articles.body: A British stunt driver and his 11-year-old son turned their shared passion for cars into a family achievement by setting three Guinness World Records during the annual Guinness World Records Day celebrations on November 19, 2026. Alastair Moffatt demonstrated his precision driving by parking a Mini Cooper on two wheels, while his son William completed 10 consecutive donuts in a drift kart in just over 17 seconds. The pair then teamed up to set their first joint record with a synchronised parking stunt. But the celebrations came with another surprise: Alastair donated the Mini Cooper he had used to break four of his world records to Guinness World Records London, allowing visitors to see the car up close.Father sets record with a Mini Cooper driven on two wheelsAlastair Moffatt, an experienced stunt driver and multiple Guinness World Records title holder, took on the challenge of performing the tightest parallel park while driving a car on two wheels.The attempt took place outside The O2 in London, where Moffatt manoeuvred his Mini Cooper into a tight parking space, leaving a combined gap of just 6.53 metres between the vehicles on either side. The stunt required precise control and balance as he brought the car down from its two-wheel position to complete the manoeuvre.Moffatt described the achievement as a way to combine two of his existing parallel-parking records with his ability to drive on two wheels. He said he wanted to make the stunt look more spectacular than a conventional handbrake turn.His 11-year-old son completes 10 drift-kart donuts in 17.14 secondsWhile his father took on the two-wheel parking challenge, William Moffatt stepped into a drift kart to attempt his own Guinness World Records title.The 11-year-old completed 10 consecutive donuts, or circular spins, in just 17.14 seconds, earning a record for the fastest time to perform the sequence in a drift kart.William has been following his father's footsteps in motorsport and said he was inspired by him. He also shared his ambition to beat his father's records and establish more achievements of his own.The young record holder encouraged others to keep practising and never give up on their goals, saying that they too could become world record holders.Father and son set their first joint Guinness World RecordThe duo then joined forces for their first-ever joint Guinness World Records attempt, taking on the tightest mirrored parallel park.William drove a classic white Mini equipped with dual controls, while Alastair manoeuvred a pillar-box red Mini. The two cars were driven into parallel parking positions simultaneously, leaving just 210 centimetres between them.The achievement added a shared record to their individual successes, turning the occasion into a father-son milestone.Alastair recalled that his previous Guinness World Records Day appearance had been 11 years earlier, when William was still in a pushchair watching him attempt a record. Seeing his son take part in the challenges alongside him made the occasion particularly meaningful.Dad donates the Mini Cooper behind four world recordsBeyond the driving achievements, Alastair made another announcement by donating the Mini Cooper he had used to break four of his world records to Guinness World Records London.The vehicle will be displayed at the organisation's new permanent entertainment attraction at The O2, giving visitors an opportunity to see the car associated with his record-breaking career.The attraction is scheduled to open on January 24, 2027. It will allow visitors to explore record-breaking achievements and attempt challenges of their own.Alastair's donation means the Mini Cooper will continue to be part of the Guinness World Records story even after its record-setting runs have ended.Guinness World Records Day celebrates achievements across the globeThe father-son duo were among several record holders who took part in the 2026 celebrations, with challenges staged in different countries.In the United States, performance painter David Garibaldi painted the Statue of Liberty in 43.5 seconds, setting a record for the fastest time to paint a landmark statue.In China, 14-year-old BMX rider Liu Haoran performed a bicycle backflip at a height of 3.13 metres. He was welcomed by the Pakistani CdA. First Pakistan minister in India since 2023 & May 2025 conflict," Abbas alleged in a post on X.However, according to sources cited by news agency ANI, a director from the Union ministry of culture and an under secretary from the Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran (PAI) division of the MEA were present at the airport to receive Malik as part of the welcome protocol.The sources also clarified that all SCO member countries arriving in New Delhi were being extended a similar level of protocol.Malik's visit is significant as he is the first Pakistani minister to travel to India in three years and the first since the May 2025 military confrontation between the two nuclear-armed countries following the Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed by Pakistan-backed terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir.The last high-profile visit by a Pakistani political leader was that of then-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari in 2023.Why is the Pakistani minister visiting IndiaMalik is in New Delhi to participate in the thematic sessions of the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, scheduled to be held from November 20 to 22.According to Pakistan's ministry of foreign affairs, Malik will represent Islamabad at the forum and present Pakistan's perspective on the importance of dialogue among civilisations and its role in diplomacy.In a statement, the ministry said the minister's address would highlight Pakistan's constructive role in the SCO, along with the country's diverse civilisational and cultural heritage."Pakistan's participation in this Forum is reflective of its contribution as an active State to promote dialogue, cooperation and understanding in line with the 'Shanghai Spirit'," the statement said.Pakistan's participation follows India's invitation to all 10 SCO member states, along with observer countries and dialogue partners, to attend the inaugural forum.The ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal had earlier confirmed that several countries, articles.title: A Scottish couple argued that a row of 17 trees and shrubs on their property was not legally a hedge, but officials rejected their appeal and ordered them to reduce its height after neighbours complained
articles.summary: A property dispute in East Lothian, Scotland, has ended with a couple being ordered to reduce the height of a row of trees and shrubs after authorities
articles.body: A property dispute in East Lothian, Scotland, has ended with a couple being ordered to reduce the height of a row of trees and shrubs after authorities ruled that the planting qualified as a high hedge under Scottish law. Professor Angus Macdonald and Dr Patricia Macdonald had challenged the order, arguing that their garden boundary consisted of 17 individual trees and shrubs rather than a hedge. However, a Scottish Government reporter upheld the council’s decision following an inspection of the properties. The case was reported by STV News and Midlothian View, with further details of Scotland’s high hedge legislation available through the Scottish Government.How the dispute beganThe disagreement arose at the couple’s property in Ashgrove, Musselburgh, which falls within the Musselburgh Conservation Area. Their neighbours approached East Lothian Council, complaining that the boundary vegetation was growing over their property, dropping leaves, berries and other debris, and significantly restricting their access to natural light.Following the complaint, East Lothian Council issued a High Hedge Notice requiring the couple to reduce the height of the planting. The Macdonalds challenged the decision before Scottish Ministers. Their appeal centred on the classification of the vegetation, maintaining that the boundary was made up of a varied collection of closely planted trees and shrubs rather than a conventional hedge.Why officials rejected the appealThe Scottish Government reporter visited the gardens before reaching a decision. Under Scotland’s High Hedges (Scotland) Act 2013, a high hedge can consist of a row of two or more trees or shrubs that exceeds two metres in height and forms a barrier to light.The legislation does not require the vegetation to consist of a single species or resemble a traditionally trimmed garden hedge. What matters is whether the planting meets the legal criteria and affects the reasonable enjoyment of neighbouring property.After examining the boundary, the reporter concluded that the trees and shrubs met the definition. The planting was found to restrict light and interfere with the neighbouring property’s reasonable enjoyment, supporting the council’s decision to issue the notice.The couple’s argument for preserving the treesThe Macdonalds also argued that removing or substantially reducing the vegetation would affect the character and environmental value of their garden. They maintained that the trees and ivy made an important contribution to the appearance of Ashgrove, particularly because the property lies within a conservation area. Their appeal highlighted the practical benefits of the planting, including protection from extreme weather, improved air quality and shade during periods of high temperatures.They also pointed to the wildlife supported by the garden, citing more than 50 species of birds, over 10 species of butterflies and numerous bees and other pollinating insects. However, the reporter concluded that the planting could continue to provide environmental and visual benefits even after its height had been reduced.What happens to the hedge now?Under the council’s notice, the boundary planting must be cut back and maintained at a maximum height of 2.5 metres, approximately eight feet. The order does not cover every tree along the boundary. An ash tree and a willow tree, positioned at opposite ends of the boundary wall, have been excluded from the required trimming.The couple have also been given additional time to complete the work. The revised compliance period is intended to ensure that the trimming takes place outside the bird-nesting season. The decision brings the appeal to a close, although it highlights how Scottish legislation can apply to mixed rows of trees and shrubs, even when property owners do not consider the planting to be a hedge.You use AI every day. articles.title: Built to beat enemy radar, why US F-22 raptor is still stuck in 1990s
articles.summary: The US Air Force's F-22 Raptor is designed to evade enemy radar, hunt down rival aircraft and dominate the skies with some of the world's most advanced
articles.body: The US Air Force's F-22 Raptor is designed to evade enemy radar, hunt down rival aircraft and dominate the skies with some of the world's most advanced combat technology.But one of America's most sophisticated stealth fighters has an unexpectedly old-school requirement: the US air Force is looking for memory cards with a minimum storage capacity of just 256 MB, using formats dating back to the 1990s.According to a procurement notice published by the US department of the air force on November 16, the F-22 programme is seeking suppliers for flash-storage cards used in its next-generation micro-Data Transfer Cartridge (mDTC) system.The requirement includes PC Standard 95 Type II flash ATA cards and CompactFlash cards with compatible adapters, each offering at least 256 MB of storage. The cards must also support reading and writing data through government-furnished equipment, the notice said.The notice, issued by the F-22 Division's modernization branch, is a market-research exercise to identify potential suppliers.What is flash storage and what does it do in the F-22?Flash storage is a type of electronic memory that can retain information even when the power is switched off. Unlike RAM, which temporarily holds data while a computer is running, flash storage preserves information for later use. It is commonly found in USB drives, memory cards and solid-state drives.CompactFlash, one of the formats specified by the US Air Force, is a removable flash-storage format introduced in 1994. The other option, PC Standard 95 Type II flash ATA cards, belongs to the older PC Card storage ecosystem.In the F-22, the storage cards are being sought for its micro-Data Transfer Cartridge (mDTC) system. The broader role of a data-transfer cartridge is to move information between ground-based equipment and the aircraft's onboard systems.A US Air Force report published in July 2019 described how F-22 maintenance specialists removed the aircraft's Data Transfer Cartridge and downloaded its stored information onto a computer to investigate technical problems and identify faults. This provides an example of how the aircraft's data-transfer system supports maintenance and troubleshooting.Why is the F-22 still using 1990s-era technology?The use of CompactFlash and PCMCIA formats in the F-22 requirement raises a larger question about how advanced military aircraft continue to operate with older electronic systems even as commercial technology moves towards newer standards.One reason is the challenge of maintaining compatibility with existing aircraft hardware. A newer storage device cannot automatically replace an older one simply because it offers greater capacity or faster data-transfer speeds. It must work with the aircraft's existing interfaces and software.The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), in a technical paper on avionics obsolescence, explains that replacing discontinued electronic components can range from substituting an equivalent part to undertaking major hardware redesigns and software recertification. Such changes must also preserve the aircraft's continued airworthiness.The problem is not unique to the F-22. A US department of defense presentation on electronics obsolescence identifies the long operational lives of military platforms, dependence on commercial electronic components and the cost and time involved in redesigning and requalifying replacement hardware as major challenges for defence programmes.The F-22 procurement notice itself reflects these concerns. The Air Force is asking potential suppliers about manufacturing origins, component traceability, counterfeit prevention, product end-of-life projections and last-time-buy policies. These questions indicate the importance of ensuring that compatible components remain available over the aircraft's service life.

articles.title: South Korea: 111 students caught with new measures against cheating at Suneung exam
articles.summary: The students were caught with banned smart devices while taking the high-stakes Suneung exam.
articles.body:
South Korea's education ministry says 111 candidates were found with unauthorised smart devices during a high-stakes nationwide exam, after officials introduced urgent measures to tackle rising cases of AI-assisted cheating.

Five of the candidates were caught red-handed using smart devices during the exam, authorities said on Friday.

Half a million students sat for the college entry exam, also known as Suneung, which took place this week under the shadow of several recent high-profile cheating scandals.

Prior to the Suneung, authorities announced anti-cheating measures such as emergency alerts sent to every single mobile phone in the country to detect unauthorised devices in exam halls.

On Friday, Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung called for an overhaul of the exam system to tackle AI-assisted cheating.

In South Korea, public examinations "significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources", Lee said, adding that using AI to cheat in such tests "rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust".

Concerns over academic dishonesty had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.

Last month, two candidates were caught cheating with AI glasses during university entrance exams.

The education ministry said earlier this month that four students across middle and high schools were caught using AI glasses to cheat this year.

These fears came to a boil over the weekend, when the top scorer of South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam admitted to cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.

His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.

"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," said the candidate, 34-year-old Han Won-seok, in a video published on Sunday.

His confession, days ahead of the Suneung, prompted authorities to introduce last-minute measures to prevent cheating during the national exam.

The measures included nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.

Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.

The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.

It was the first time that South Korea tapped on its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.

Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.

All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times that he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.

Another told news outlet Yonhap that he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

Held every November, the Suneung is an infamous eight-hour marathon of back-to-back exams.

Students attempt about 200 questions across various subjects, which include Korean, maths, English, social and natural sciences, among others.

The country itself comes to a standstill - construction work halts, planes are grounded and military training gets suspended to facilitate an optimal testing environment.

Many South Koreans see the Suneung as a culmination of years of formal education - and a turning point that determines their university placements, careers, and social statuses.

articles.title: AI has decoded 1,009 pages of Kurt Gödel’s secret notebooks, uncovering 663 theorems and ideas, including a near-complete proof of a major mathematical problem left unfinished in the 1940s
articles.summary: Kurt Gödel’s 1,009 pages of secret notebooks, decoded with artificial intelligence, have revealed hundreds of unknown theorems and 14 unexplored themes in
articles.body: Kurt Gödel’s 1,009 pages of secret notebooks, decoded with artificial intelligence, have revealed hundreds of unknown theorems and 14 unexplored themes in mathematics and logic. Finnish logician Jan von Plato of the University of Helsinki asked Anthropic’s Claude to read the workbooks Gödel filled in the early 1940s, and within days it returned a 650-page explanation. Among the findings is an almost complete argument for the independence of the axiom of choice. Von Plato says the workbooks also contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 1970s and 1980s, and that Gödel was far ahead of his time.Why AI decoded Kurt Gödel’s 1,009 pages of unpublished notebooks matter to mathematics and modern computingAccording to The Guardian, the Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age. They showed that in every mathematical system there are true statements that can be neither proved nor disproved, an insight that inspired Alan Turing’s 1936 paper, which began the theory of modern computation.Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis in 1940, settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute for Advanced Study. After his landmark results of the 1930s, he published only a few papers, but his unpublished work runs to tens of thousands of pages. Among it are 16 notebooks written in the early 1940s, known as the workbooks, which hold 1,009 pages of dense writing on mathematics and logic. Much of it is in Gabelsberger, a German shorthand that was already obsolete when Gödel used it.Jan von Plato has been decoding Kurt Gödel’s mysterious notebooks since 2017Since 2017, von Plato has led a project at the University of Helsinki to understand the workbooks. He secured a grant of €2.5 million (£2.1 million) from the European Research Council, taught himself the shorthand and assembled a small team. Even so, progress on the mathematics was painfully slow, at about a page a week.The turning point came in August, at a conference in France on artificial intelligence and theorem proving, where computer scientists suggested he enlist Claude. Back in Helsinki in September, he showed the model his transcriptions of the workbooks, six books he had written on Gödel and other scientific literature.Claude read 1,009 pages of Gödel’s notebooks and produced a 650-page digest in daysWithin a couple of days, Claude had produced a comprehensive digest of the entire material, which revealed that Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about. Von Plato told The Guardian that the explanation had to be checked page by page, but that it is basically a work impossible for human beings to produce. People read one page at a time and tend to forget things, he said, whereas the model can connect all the pieces across a thousand pages and see Gödel’s writings as one piece. He then asked Claude to extract every theorem for which Gödel had a proof, a sketched proof or an idea for a proof. It found 663.Why researchers combined AI with a strict system to check Gödel’s workVon Plato put those results into Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs. About 400 were verified as stated. About 200 were repaired, meaning the statement had to be made more precise or an assumption added. About 50 were false, which is unsurprising, because Gödel himself sometimes marked passages in the margins of his notes as incorrect or bad.The AI for Developing Countries Forum argued in its analysis that this combination is the real breakthrough. The model acted as a bridge that connected references across thousands of pages, while Coq enforced strict logical validity. The Forum described this hybrid of a language model and a formal proof checker as a template for recovering scientific knowledge without diluting mathematical standards.Gödel came one step before proving the independence of the axiom of choice, before Paul CohenIn 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields Medal, the highest honour in mathematics, for showing the independence of two famous statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice. Gödel reacted by saying he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when his peers pushed him for a proof, he could not reconstruct one from his notes.The first task von Plato gave Claude was to check whether the workbooks held a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice. The answer was almost. In the same interview, von Plato said Gödel was “just one step away”. One definition was wrong, but Gödel had written the right one two years earlier, so he would probably have reached the correct version within months. When Claude presented the reconstructed proof, von Plato ran it through Coq, and it passed. He described the architecture of the proof as wonderful, because it makes all the set theory results follow a uniform pattern.In the same report, Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame in Indiana, said he has not seen Claude’s reconstruction. If it stands up, he said, it is remarkable and historically interesting, though how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for historians. Resemblance to Cohen’s proof does not mean Gödel had it, he cautioned. It shows he was on the path, but credit does not go to work you tell nobody about.The 14 unexplored themes in logic and dozens of early anticipationsVon Plato said he was flabbergasted by what the digest revealed. The workbooks contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued, and Claude puts it as more than a dozen themes in logic and the foundations of mathematics that have gone unfound in the 80-plus years since they were written down.Gödel, von Plato said, starts from very clear ideas and then proceeds methodically, step after step, rather than playing with formulas and hoping to arrive somewhere. He is sure that continued study will reveal further treasures, and he plans to explore Gödel’s physics and cosmology notebooks, which he calls unknown territory, once his current logic projects are finished.Why the Gödel decoding method could help recover neglected archives in developing countriesThe AI for Developing Countries Forum argued that the workflow could matter well beyond mathematics. Across Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, it noted, millions of pages of scientific, medical and legal manuscripts sit unstudied in national archives. Many are written in obsolete scripts, such as classical Arabic variants, Ottoman Turkish, Ge’ez, pre-modern Tamil or Mesoamerican scripts, and trained paleographers are scarce. If the approach can be adapted to low-cost, openly available models, the Forum said, developing nations would no longer depend only on well-funded Western universities to decipher their own records.It also stressed that the method rested on deep human expertise, since years of painstaking transcription came before the model could synthesise anything. It suggested watching for the peer-reviewed release of the full synthesis and the Coq files, for von Plato’s move to the physics and cosmology notebooks, and for open-source projects that pair language models with low-resource scripts.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Africa crime statistics: Nearly 600 women killed within three months
articles.summary: Police officials called for "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.
articles.body:
Nearly 600 women were killed in South Africa between July and September this year, according to the country's latest crime statistics.

This figure includes 13 women whose partially naked and bruised bodies were found dumped in public areas in and around Johannesburg.

The murders triggered national outrage and police faced pressure to find the culprits, in a country with one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and murder rates in the world.

In the latest shocking killing, five women and a toddler were gunned down in Free State province earlier this week.

The latest crime statistics, released on Friday, revealed that 581 women were killed in the country between July and September, including 131 in the Gauteng province which includes Johannesburg.

The same statistics revealed a slight decline in the number of murders.

Police reported 5,590 murders, 204 fewer than in the same period last year. This still come to an average of about 60 murders a day.

It is not clear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease because the police had stopped giving these figures recently due to what they said were "significant anomalies" in the statistics.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said there needed to be "greater efforts to prevent... violence" against women and children.

According to police in Free State province, south of Johannesburg, three masked men opened fire on a family in the township of Botshabelo on Wednesday night.

The trio were allegedly looking for the owner of the house and when they realised he was not there, "forced their way into the house and started shooting at the people inside", police said.

The owner's wife was also shot in the stomach and was taken to hospital. No arrests have been made.

On Thursday, the police chief for Gauteng province said that eight people had now been arrested in relations to the 13 murders which sparked a national outcry earlier this year.

General Tommy Mthombeni said three of the arrests related to the murder of Elizabeth Moselakgomo, an avid runner whose disappearance prompted a highly publicised nationwide search for her.

The 38-year-old went missing while out for her daily run near her home in Kempton Park.

Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September.

The police chief said two other people had been detained in connection with the death of Jabulile Ntimba, 33, who was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. Ntimba's was the ninth body found in the Ekurhuleni region.

He said another person had been arrested for one of the Kempton Park cases while a suspect was arrested over Ntombifuthi Nxumalo's death in Tembisa, north-east of central Johannesburg.

Nxumalo was discovered at a cemetery on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.

Another arrest was made back in July, in relation to the death of Busisiwe Mahlangu, whose body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July. Hers was the first of the 13 bodies discovered in the area.

In September, President Cyril Ramaphosa vowed that "no stone will be left unturned" to find those behind the killings.
